title: The Bottleneck in a Wafer Fab Isn't the Lithography Machine—It's the OHT Robots on the Ceiling
dek: The real capacity constraint in a wafer fab isn't just the lithography machine—it's the OHT vehicles scurrying along the ceiling. The 300mm transition made them indispensable, and today the market is a duopoly of Daifuku and Muratec.
why: The rarely discussed AMHS segment involves floor costs, injury data, and a Daifuku/Muratec duopoly. It fills in the missing piece beyond the lithography narrative.
who: Wafer fab manufacturing and automation engineers, semiconductor equipment investors, and anyone wanting to understand the hidden costs in advanced-node capacity stories.
skip: Daifuku's pre-WWII founding history can be fast-forwarded; jump straight to the industry consolidation conclusion at 18:38.

points.h: The fab's handling problem is predetermined by the bay layout
points.body: Fabs are divided into sub-areas by processing zone, and within each zone, tools are arranged in bays. Movement within a bay is called intrabay; movement between bays is interbay. Each bay is equipped with stockers—automated parking towers that hold roughly 150–250 FOUPs. Stockers replaced open shelving, saving cleanroom floor space, helping track work-in-progress, and serving as buffers and zone entry/exit points. The entire handling problem grows out of this layout.

points.h: Cleanroom floors are too expensive, so handling went to the ceiling
points.body: Once wafers leave a tool, they must be kept in FOUPs; dust can ruin them. Early on, people pushed FOUPs between bays, but a single lot could be worth $100,000, so automation began in the 1980s. First came floor-bound AGVs, limited to about 1 ft/s for safety; then rail-guided RGVs were faster but took up floor space and required guarding. PRI's Aerotrak hung a monorail from the ceiling, and by 1988 such interbay AMHS was common. Cleanroom floors are expensive, so this move was inevitable.

points.h: After interbay automation, humans became the new bottleneck
points.body: Once interbay was automated, the bottleneck shifted to operators manually moving FOUPs from stockers to tools. A skilled operator takes 30–90 seconds per load change, but a bay has many tools. The author recalls hearing constant beeping in a DRAM fab, told it was tools demanding operator attention. Intrabay automation must sense tool processing status and load/unload automatically; any misalignment or timing error stops the tool. In the early days there were no industry standards, so each company invented its own. Hot lots and SUPER hot lots, being troublesome to program, were often still carried by operators on the run.

points.h: 300mm wasn't an upgrade—it was an ultimatum for automation
points.body: The shift to 300mm wafers in the late 1990s made manual handling unsustainable. SEMATECH found that 15–20% of tool time in older fabs was wasted waiting for operators or FOUPs; tools were more expensive, heavier, and took more floor space. A full 300mm FOUP weighs about 9 kg, exceeding the 'maximum acceptable weight' for repetitive lifting in ergonomics. A survey of Taiwanese 200mm fabs found 40–60% of workers had shoulder discomfort and 30–50% had back problems. High-volume 300mm bays need over 300 moves per hour, versus 125–175 in older fabs—automation was the only option.

points.h: OHT won by not using floor space, not by being faster
points.body: The core of second-generation AMHS is the OHT: vehicles run on overhead rails directly above tools and use a hoist to pick and place FOUPs at the tool's front-end interface, completing the move in seconds at up to 60 m/min. It doesn't take floor space or compete with people, but it's expensive to install, inflexible in routing, and hanging over tools carries a contamination risk. To address this, SEMI established common standards for loadport configuration and optical signal exchange between vehicle and tool, ensuring handoffs succeed and saving costs. OHT became the only choice for a unified system.

points.h: A system can cost over $100 million, so most fabs kept using people
points.body: TSMC was among the first to open a 300mm fab with full-roof AMHS: Hsinchu Fab 12, which started at 150nm and later moved to 130nm, with 2,000 vehicles making 600,000 moves per day. But the scale and cost are daunting—a complete 300mm interbay/intrabay system runs $50–100 million and takes two years to install. For years afterward, many fabs still relied on manual wafer handling. Automation wasn't a one-time switch.

points.h: AMHS scheduling has no optimal solution, only trade-offs
points.body: Scheduling is done centrally by the fab's control system: assigning vehicles, planning routes, handling congestion, and avoiding deadlocks and down tools. Fabs don't add vehicles for peak times; they work with what they have. Hot lots and rework must be encoded as special rules. The author's verdict: there is no optimal algorithm. So operators use simulation to optimize targets like average delivery time, on-time delivery rate, cycle time, or throughput. It's like designing a traffic system for the entire fab.

points.h: The 300mm transition reshuffled the OHT supplier landscape
points.body: Daifuku (大福) is the largest OHT supplier. Its predecessor made steel forging machinery and renamed itself after WWII to avoid zaibatsu dissolution, taking the name from the first characters of its Osaka and Fukuchiyama plants. The turning point was licensing chain conveyor technology from Jervis B. Webb, supplying Toyota's Motomachi plant in 1959 and growing with Japan's automakers. The 300mm transition reset the market: PRI, struggling with Aeroloader development costs, was sold to Brooks Automation for $500 million; eventually Daifuku and Muratec consolidated the industry and have dominated it ever since.

terms.def: The collective automated equipment for moving FOUPs within a fab, including AGVs, OHTs, and stockers.
A standardized wafer container, typically holding 25 wafers, used for safe transport between tools.
A vehicle that runs on overhead rails and uses a hoist to pick and place FOUPs at tool front-end interfaces.
An automated storage and retrieval machine, like an automated parking tower, used as a buffer and zone entry/exit.
Interbay refers to transport between bays; intrabay refers to transport between tools within the same bay.

quotes.text: The first things you will notice upon stepping inside a fab clean room are the equipment. Massive, inscrutable, expensive. But the second things you will notice are the little vehicles puttering around on the ceiling above your head.
I was told that it was because the tool wants to let the operator know that it needs its diaper, sorry wafers, changed.
They even have SUPER hot lots which represent the absolute first priority for every tool and operator on the line.
A study done by SEMATECH in the mid-1990s discovered that in older fabs, 15-20% of tool time is wasted waiting for an operator or FOUP to arrive.

The OHT vehicle aligns itself above the tool. And then it lowers a hoist to either pick up or drop off the FOUP right from the tool's frontend interface. It is magnificent to watch and just takes a few seconds.
In the end, Daifuku and Muratec consolidated the industry between themselves and they dominate it to this day.
